title: Why Target Ranking Is Not Enough in Immuno-Oncology
text:
Target-discovery workflows often end with a familiar output: a table of genes ordered by a composite score. The highest-ranked genes are then treated as the most promising candidates.
That is useful, but incomplete.
A gene can be strongly associated with melanoma and still be unsuitable as a direct therapeutic target. Another gene may have only moderate disease-association evidence but be highly relevant as a resistance biomarker, a combination partner, or a marker of a specific suppressive cell population.
The central problem is therefore not only:

Which genes are associated with the disease?

It is also:

What translational role does each gene play, and under which therapeutic intent should it be prioritised?

This distinction motivated TargetIntel-IO, an explainable framework for triaging candidate genes in anti-PD-1-resistant melanoma.

title: Why Target Ranking Is Not Enough in Immuno-Oncology
text:
One gene, several possible meanings
Consider four familiar genes:








Gene
Biological relevance
Translational interpretation




LAG3
Alternative immune checkpoint
Potential combination target with PD-1 blockade


B2M
Antigen-presentation machinery
Resistance mechanism and biomarker, not necessarily a direct target


BRAF
Tumor-intrinsic melanoma driver
Strong fit for small-molecule intervention


CDKN2A
Tumor-suppressor biology
Mechanistically important but difficult to restore directly



A single universal score may place all four genes in the same list. But a scientist deciding which antibody to develop, which biomarker to measure, or which tumor-intrinsic dependency to inhibit is asking three different questions.
TargetIntel-IO therefore separates the problem into three intent-specific rankings:

Antibody and immuno-oncology combination targets
Resistance biomarkers
Tumor-intrinsic and small-molecule targets

The goal is not to create more scores for their own sake. It is to make the biological decision represented by each score explicit.

title: Why Target Ranking Is Not Enough in Immuno-Oncology
text:
The architecture: rules before rhetoric
The current version of TargetIntel-IO is deliberately transparent. It does not ask a language model to decide whether a gene is a good target. Instead, it applies an auditable sequence of steps.





flowchart TD
    A[Disease-associated genes] --> B[Resistance-axis annotation]
    B --> C[Stable biological role]
    C --> D[Therapeutic direction]
    D --> E[Modality fit]
    E --> F1[Antibody / IO score]
    E --> F2[Biomarker score]
    E --> F3[Small-molecule score]
    F1 --> G[Evidence for / against]
    F2 --> G
    F3 --> G
    G --> H[Confidence and hypothesis card]






The distinction between a stable role and an intent-specific ranking is important.
For example, B2M remains part of antigen-presentation biology regardless of which ranking is being inspected. What changes is its usefulness under a particular objective. It may rank highly as a resistance biomarker while remaining a poor direct therapeutic target.

section: What the system does not claim

title: Why Target Ranking Is Not Enough in Immuno-Oncology
section: Why build the transparent core first?
text:
Why build the transparent core first?
It would be easy to begin with a large language model that reads papers and produces polished summaries. But fluent text does not guarantee that the underlying evidence is correct, independent, or relevant.
A more defensible architecture is:
structured evidence
        ↓
deterministic classification and scoring
        ↓
traceable target card
        ↓
optional language-model synthesis
In that design, a language model can eventually help retrieve literature, identify contradictions, and explain the evidence. It should not silently replace the evidence or the decision logic.

title: Why Target Ranking Is Not Enough in Immuno-Oncology
text:
What comes next
The next scientifically meaningful step is not to add every available omics modality at once. It is to introduce one carefully selected external evidence layer and test whether it changes the conclusions in a useful way.
A public cohort of patients treated with anti-PD-1 would allow us to ask:

Are the proposed resistance biomarkers associated with response?
Do combination-target candidates show coherent clinical patterns?
Which classifications are contradicted by external data?
Does the additional evidence improve confidence or merely duplicate existing knowledge?

Later extensions could add functional dependency, single-cell expression, spatial organisation, and structured literature evidence. Each layer should earn its place through an ablation analysis rather than being included because it is fashionable.

title: Why Target Ranking Is Not Enough in Immuno-Oncology
text:
The broader lesson
Target prioritisation is not only a ranking problem. It is a problem of role, context, modality, uncertainty, and therapeutic intent.
A useful system should therefore do more than say:

Gene A ranks above Gene B.

It should explain:

Gene A is a plausible combination target because of this mechanism and modality, whereas Gene B is more useful as a resistance biomarker and should not be interpreted as a direct therapeutic target.

That is the principle behind TargetIntel-IO: not replacing scientific reasoning with a score, but making the reasoning easier to inspect.

title: TargetIntel-IO
text:
The problem
A gene can be highly relevant to disease and still be the wrong direct therapeutic target. In anti-PD-1-resistant melanoma, the same candidate might instead be a resistance biomarker, an immune-context marker, a tumour-intrinsic dependency or a mechanism with poor tractability.
TargetIntel-IO does not compress those possibilities into one universal score. It asks a more useful question: valuable for what therapeutic purpose?

title: TargetIntel-IO
text:
What the tool does
The platform retrieves and structures evidence, assigns stable biological roles, and produces separate rankings for:

Antibody / IO combination strategies;
Resistance biomarker strategies;
Tumour-intrinsic small-molecule strategies.






flowchart LR
    A[Open Targets + curated rules] --> B[Deterministic features]
    B --> C[Stable role]
    C --> D[Three intent rankings]
    D --> E[Cards, reports and figures]
    F[Reviewed evidence] --> G[Read-only report layers]
    H[DepMap 26Q1] --> G
    G --> E






The deterministic baseline remains authoritative. Optional evidence, feasibility and functional-dependency layers can decorate a report, but they cannot silently change baseline features, roles, scores or ranks.

Scientific boundary
TargetIntel-IO is research-use software. It does not recommend treatment, establish causality, validate a therapeutic target or biomarker, or predict patient response. The immediate future direction is external validation with public clinical response cohorts and single-cell/spatial context while preserving the same evidence boundaries.

text:
Data and modelling





flowchart LR
    A[DepMap expression, mutation, copy number] --> C[Stable ModelID join]
    B[PRISM drug-response AUC] --> C
    C --> D[Grouped split + training-only selection]
    D --> E[Baselines + Elastic Net + XGBoost]
    E --> F[Calibration, conformal interval, OOD, SHAP]
    F --> G[Locked GDSC2 validation]






The safeguards are central to the project:

The same cell line cannot appear in both training and test data.
Test data never select genes.
GDSC2 is locked and cannot tune the model.
XGBoost is compared against lineage-only and Elastic Net baselines.
Weak results remain visible instead of being reframed as successes.

title: Dev Autopilot
text:
The problem
AI coding agents can produce useful work, but a scientific software project also needs durable state, explicit permissions, reproducible tests, independent review and a clear boundary around human authority.
Dev Autopilot turns those requirements into a workflow instead of relying on one long prompt or one agent grading its own work.

title: Dev Autopilot
text:
Authority is separated





flowchart LR
    A[Planning advice] --> B[Implementation]
    B --> C[Deterministic gates]
    C --> D[Adversarial audit]
    D --> E[Independent review]
    E --> F[Bounded correction]
    F --> C
    E --> G[Ready for human review]






Planning advice is not approval. The implementation agent cannot approve its own diff. Review agents cannot override mechanical gates. The system stops at READY_FOR_HUMAN_REVIEW, leaving commit, pull-request and merge decisions to a person.

section: Why it belongs in a scientific portfolio
text:
Why it belongs in a scientific portfolio
The project is not a claim that automation removes scientific judgment. It demonstrates the opposite: agentic workflows become more useful when scientific scope, mechanical correctness, adversarial review and human authority are represented as different responsibilities.

title: MTF Prediction
text:
The scientific question
Some membrane proteins release intracellular fragments that participate in nuclear signalling. Could topological domains of mammalian membrane proteins contain sequence patterns that a deep-learning model recognises as transcription-factor-like?
MTF Prediction is a research-analysis archive built to generate candidates and explore how strongly the result depends on protein-domain boundaries.

title: MTF Prediction
text:
Analysis design
Reviewed human and mouse membrane proteins from UniProtKB 2022_05 were separated into cytoplasmic, extracellular and lumenal domains. Each eligible domain was evaluated under three boundary definitions:







Condition
Sequence submitted to the model




No TMD
Annotated topological domain only


Half TMD
Domain extended by approximately half of each adjacent transmembrane segment


Full TMD
Domain extended across the complete adjacent transmembrane segment








flowchart LR
    A[UniProtKB topology] --> B[Cytoplasmic, extracellular, lumenal]
    B --> C[No, half or full TMD]
    C --> D[Coordinate-aware FASTA]
    D --> E[DeepTFactor]
    E --> F[Candidate predictions]
    F --> G[Captum Integrated Gradients]

title: MTF Prediction
MTF Prediction
text:
What the project demonstrates
This project connects biological annotation, command-line data processing, protein deep learning and model interpretation. It also exposes a biologically important sensitivity question: if a prediction changes when the boundary moves by a few residues, it should be interpreted differently from one that is stable across all three definitions.

title: MTF Prediction
text:
Scientific boundary
A positive prediction only means that a fragment contains sequence features associated with transcription factors by the selected model. It does not establish DNA binding, nuclear localisation, proteolytic activation or transcriptional function in vivo. Orthogonal experimental validation is required.
The repository is a research archive, not a packaged end-to-end application, and remains tied to the 2022_05 UniProtKB release and the original DeepTFactor checkpoint.


Explore the full analysis matrix, processed inputs and residue-attribution outputs.
